newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-German shares fall sharply, dollar slips.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German shares fall sharply, dollar slips.

text.p: European markets largely ignored the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping on Thursday, but the German bourse went into sharp decline as investors appeared to have decided the market had risen far enough for now.

The dollar was initially bid up in Europe with Deng's death having a muted impact, but it eased against the mark following a strong business climate report in Germany and an unexpectadly buoyant Philadelphia Fed index in the United States.
European markets focused mainly on local factors, while Asian investors marked prices mostly higher in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan as Deng's death removed some uncertainty.
Traders in Europe appeared more concerned about economic data coming out of Germany, however.
As expected, the German Bundesbank decided to leave interest rates unchanged after releasing money supply data showing strong growth in January.
The country's Ifo economic institute earlier said its west German business climate index jumped to 93.3 in January from 90.9 in December, indicating confidence was growing.
And German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt predicted Europe's largest economy would continue to recover this year.
"We are standing by our forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth," Rexrodt told parliament during a debate of the government's annual economic report.
Despite the bullish sounds from Rexrodt, German shares fell one percent in bourse trade and continued to drop in later screen-based business as Wall Street fell in early business.
Jitters ahead of Friday's expiry of options contracts added to the volatility.
The 30-share DAX index ended bourse trade down 37.72 points at 3,196.03, while the IBIS DAX index that reflects screen based business was down 14 points.

On foreign exchange markets, the dollar was bid up to around 1.7000 marks in early trade,declined to around 1.6828 and then rebounded to 1.6917 by 1530 GMT. Against the yen it slipped to 123.62 before rebounding one yen.
U.S. data showed weekly jobless claims nudged higher last week, while construction starts rose slightly in January.
However, analysts said the big focus for the market was the semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, which U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan will deliver to Congress on February 26 and 27.
The London stock market opened the day showing losses like its main European rivals, but the market later recovered to post a fresh intraday high of 4,362.4.
"We hit a new high, but it didn't feel like it. We're just struggling to maintain these levels," said one dealer.
Dealers said they were awaiting the opening of Wall Street for direction. Government bonds trimmed their opening losses, which helped support shares, dealers said.
Both companies declined comment on the latest bout of market rumour.
French stocks traded lower through the morning as the market continued to digest its recent gains.
"It's a small consolidation and it's occurring calmly," a trader said. "None of the blue chip CAC issues is losing much more than two percent. It's profit taking affecting the whole of the market."
Although the CAC-40 index was down 21 points at 2,573 by 1530 GMT, traders said the bourse's weakness did not put in doubt the market's broadly rising trend.
CURRENCIES AT 1530 GMT
The dollar was quoted as 1.6917 marks and 123.15 yen, compared with 1.6979 marks and 124.35 yen in late European trading on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1550 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 6.4 points, or 0.15 percent, at 4,351.0.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 21.31 points, or 0.7 percent, at 2,573.45.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended down 37.72 to 3,196.03 points. The IBIS DAX was down 14 points at 3,195.05.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed in the afternoon at $345.0 against 344.85 in the morning.
